title: Fitting a concealed-cistern back-to-wall toilet
subtitle: Install a wall-hung or back-to-wall toilet with the flushing cistern hidden inside a carrier frame or timber boxing behind the wall
excerpt: How to fit a concealed-cistern toilet system. Covers fixing the cistern carrier frame, connecting the water supply, setting the cistern height, connecting the waste, boxing in the cistern, and setting the flush volume.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK trade plumbing and sanitary ware installation practice. Water Regulations Advisory Scheme (WRAS) guidance (open access).

glossaryTerms.definition: A toilet flushing cistern designed to be hidden inside a wall frame, ducting boxing, or within the toilet unit itself. The cistern is connected to the water supply and waste behind the wall finish; only the flush plate or push button is visible on the face. Most concealed cisterns are dual-flush and are factory set to 6 and 4 litre volumes.

The panel mounted on the wall or boxing face above a concealed cistern that allows the user to actuate the flush. It clips or screws onto the front of the cistern frame and connects to the flush valve via a push rod. Available in chrome, brushed stainless, and other finishes.

A curved section of soil pipe below a toilet pan that retains a water seal to prevent sewer gases entering the room. For a back-to-wall toilet, the p-trap outlet enters the wall horizontally, connecting to the soil stack concealed in the wall. The height of the pan outlet must align exactly with the concealed waste connection.

Assemble the carrier frame following the manufacturer's instructions. Fix it to the floor and wall at the correct height for the pan outlet. The pan outlet centre height must align with the

or concealed waste connection in the wall. Use the spirit level to check the frame is plumb in both directions before fixing it tight. The frame must be solid: it carries the full weight of the pan and any seated load.

Turn off the water supply. Run a 15 mm cold water supply to the cistern inlet, cutting to length with the pipe cutter. Connect the supply tube to the cistern inlet valve using the isolating valve supplied, wrapping male threads with PTFE tape. Tighten all connections firmly. Leave the isolating valve closed until testing.

Connect the waste pan connector from the frame outlet to the concealed soil pipe, checking that the connection is push-fit and secure. The waste run must have a minimum gradient of 18 mm per metre. Before boxing in, run water through the cistern by opening the isolating valve, flushing once, and checking all connections for leaks.
Box in and fit the flush plate

Build the boxing in front of the cistern from moisture-resistant plywood or tile backer board, leaving the access panel position clear for the flush plate opening. Tile or plaster the boxing face. Fit the flush plate into the opening and connect the push rods to the cistern actuator. Set the flush volume using the adjusters on the cistern fill valve to 6 litres for full flush and 4 litres for reduced flush.

attrs.symptom: Cistern continues to run after flushing
attrs.cause: The fill valve is not seating properly, or the float is set too high and water is entering the overflow.
attrs.fix: Adjust the float level on the fill valve so the water stops about 25 mm below the overflow tube. If the valve body is faulty, replace the fill valve.

attrs.symptom: Flush plate does not operate the cistern
attrs.cause: The push rods connecting the flush plate to the actuator are not correctly aligned or are the wrong length.
attrs.fix: Remove the flush plate, check the rod lengths match the frame depth, and adjust the rod length if the cistern type allows it.
